title: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A safety committee wants one framework that simultaneously targets preventable harm, evidence-based care, patient preferences, delays, waste, and unequal treatment. Which framework fits all six aims?
questions.explanation: The Institute of Medicine's six quality aims are safe, effective, patient-centered, timely, efficient, and equitable care. Because the scenario explicitly spans preventable harm, evidence, preferences, delay, waste, and disparity, the six-domain framework is the only choice that captures all targets together.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A patient becomes hypoglycemic after a four-hour preop delay caused by scheduling failure, although the eventual treatment is correct. Which quality aim was most directly violated?
questions.explanation: Timeliness addresses harmful waits and delays in receiving needed care. The eventual treatment may be clinically correct, but a scheduling delay that causes hypoglycemia still represents a quality failure because care was not delivered when needed.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A department routinely opens airway kits that are never used and then discards them. Which quality aim is most directly compromised even if no patient is harmed?
questions.explanation: Efficiency means avoiding waste of equipment, supplies, time, and other resources while preserving quality. Routinely opening and discarding unused airway kits consumes resources without adding patient benefit, so the primary domain affected is efficiency.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: Two clinically identical patients request epidural analgesia, but one is denied solely because of insurance status. Which quality aim is violated?
questions.explanation: Equity requires that care quality not differ because of socioeconomic or other nonclinical characteristics. Denying an otherwise appropriate epidural solely because of insurance status creates a treatment difference unrelated to medical need.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A cheaper perioperative regimen is chosen despite evidence that it produces worse outcomes than the recommended treatment. Which quality domain is most directly violated?
questions.explanation: Effectiveness means providing care supported by the best available evidence to patients likely to benefit and avoiding inferior care simply because it is cheaper. Choosing a knowingly worse regimen therefore primarily violates effectiveness.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A medically reasonable sedative plan is chosen without discussing a patient's clearly stated preference to avoid that medication. Which quality domain is most directly compromised?
questions.explanation: Patient-centered care incorporates the patient's preferences, needs, and values into clinically appropriate decisions. A medically reasonable plan can still fail this domain if a clearly stated preference is ignored without discussion.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: Barcode medication scanning is introduced even though it adds a small workflow delay. Which quality aim is the intervention primarily intended to improve?
questions.explanation: Barcode scanning is a defensive system intended to prevent wrong-patient, wrong-drug, wrong-dose, and related medication errors. Its primary quality target is safety even if the verification step modestly slows workflow.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A department is tracing the foundation of the modern US patient-safety movement. Which pair of landmark IOM reports should anchor the review?
options: The WHO Surgical Safety Checklist and APSF priorities
Healthy People 2030 and the National Healthcare Quality Report
The Belmont Report and the AANA Code of Ethics
To Err Is Human (1999) and Crossing the Quality Chasm (2001)
questions.explanation: To Err Is Human (1999) brought national attention to preventable harm and systems-based patient safety, while Crossing the Quality Chasm (2001) articulated broader aims for healthcare quality. Together they are foundational Institute of Medicine reports in the modern U.S. quality movement.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A safety lecture compares the IOM upper estimate of 98,000 annual deaths from medical error with a later estimate of about 400,000. Roughly how many times larger is the later upper estimate?
questions.explanation: Dividing 400,000 by 98,000 gives about 4.1, so the later upper estimate is roughly four times the IOM figure. Later analyses gave values of about 250,000 to 400,000, but these are method-dependent estimates rather than a single definitive count, so they should be cited with their source and period.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: When comparing historical patient-safety estimates, which annual mortality range belongs specifically to the original IOM report rather than later higher estimates?
questions.explanation: To Err Is Human cited an estimated 44,000 to 98,000 annual hospital deaths associated with preventable medical errors based on studies available at the time. Later analyses used different methods and produced higher figures, so the ranges should not be conflated.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: One case involves a mislabeled syringe; another involves choosing the wrong drug because the allergy history was misunderstood. What do the two events have in common?
options: Both are execution errors at the point of use
Both are planning errors from poor knowledge
Both are errors: one execution, one planning
Both are adverse events rather than errors
questions.explanation: A medical error occurs when a correct plan is carried out incorrectly (execution) or when the plan itself is wrong (planning). The mislabeled syringe is an execution failure, while choosing the wrong drug from a misunderstood allergy history is a planning failure. Neither requires harm to count as an error, so calling them adverse events misses the point.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A wrong-medication event occurs after look-alike labeling, interruptions, and a skipped independent check. Which interpretation best reflects modern patient-safety thinking?
options: An active error within system conditions
A pure skill-based slip by one person
A latent error with no active component
A diagnostic error in drug selection
questions.explanation: Modern safety science sees the final wrong administration as an active error made possible by latent conditions such as look-alike labels, interruptions, and a skipped check. Calling it one person's slip ignores those conditions, and the latent factors alone did not give the drug. Drug selection was not the failure here, so it is not a diagnostic error.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A chest radiograph is obtained on time, but pneumonia is missed because the image is interpreted incorrectly. Which error category best fits the primary failure?
questions.explanation: The diagnostic process includes obtaining, interpreting, and acting on diagnostic information. The image was obtained on time, but incorrect interpretation caused the diagnosis to be missed, making diagnostic error the primary category.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: The intended medication is correctly selected in the plan, but a different medication is administered because two syringes were confused. Which error category best describes the event?
questions.explanation: The therapeutic plan selected the correct medication, but administration of a different syringe caused the failure during treatment delivery. Classification as a treatment error identifies where the failure manifested; systems analysis should still examine why the confusion was possible.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A serious allergy is identified correctly in preop, but the information is lost during handoff and the OR team never sees it. Which error category best captures the primary failure?
questions.explanation: The allergy was identified correctly but failed to reach the clinicians who needed it. That makes information transfer and handoff the primary failure, illustrating how communication breakdown can defeat otherwise accurate assessment.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: The team knowingly skips the routine anesthesia-machine checkout, and a hazard it would have caught reaches the patient. Which error category best fits?
questions.explanation: Routine equipment checks are preventive defenses intended to detect hazards before patient exposure. Knowingly bypassing the anesthesia-machine checkout removes that defense, so the primary failure is preventive rather than diagnostic or therapeutic.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A 10-fold vasopressor overdose causes only transient hypertension without lasting injury. Which professional obligation remains?
options: Disclose the error to the patient
Disclose only if permanent harm occurred
Report internally but do not inform the patient
Leave disclosure entirely to the surgeon
questions.explanation: Absence of permanent injury does not erase a clinically meaningful medication error. Transparent disclosure should follow professional and institutional standards and explain what occurred, known consequences, current condition, and next steps without speculation.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: Barcode scanning, pharmacy verification, and an independent double-check all exist to stop the same medication error. In the Swiss cheese model, what do these safeguards represent?
questions.explanation: In Reason's Swiss cheese model, each verification process is a separate defensive layer, or slice, intended to intercept a hazard. Redundancy matters because one layer can fail while another still stops the error.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: The barcode scanner is broken, pharmacy staffing is thin, and the independent double-check is skipped. In the Swiss cheese model, what do these weaknesses represent?
questions.explanation: The holes are weaknesses or failures within otherwise protective layers. A broken scanner, inadequate staffing, and skipped double-check become dangerous when their vulnerabilities align so no remaining defense stops the hazard.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: Wrong-site surgery occurs because small weaknesses in site marking, consent verification, and the time-out align in the same case. Which concept best explains the event?
options: A single latent condition in consent
questions.explanation: The Swiss cheese model explains harm as a hazard passing through several imperfect defenses when their weaknesses line up. Site marking, consent verification, and the time-out each had a hole, and only their alignment let wrong-site surgery happen. Blaming one layer, one person, or one latent condition misses that no single failure was enough.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: After a wrong-drug event, a root cause analysis separates the front-line slip from hidden weaknesses such as a broken scanner and thin pharmacy staffing. Whose model is being applied?
questions.explanation: James Reason's Swiss cheese model separates active failures by front-line staff from latent conditions in the system and shows harm occurring when holes in several defenses align. Donabedian's model evaluates quality through structure, process, and outcome, PDSA guides improvement cycles, and the Triple Aim sets system goals rather than explaining errors.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A wrong-drug event follows an incorrect pharmacy label, skipped double-check, and broken barcode scanner. Which interpretation best matches the Swiss cheese model?
options: Any one failed layer would cause harm
A single active failure at the bedside
One latent condition causing the event
questions.explanation: In the Swiss cheese model, harm reaches the patient when several defenses fail at once, here a wrong pharmacy label, a skipped double-check, and a broken scanner. Any one failure alone would usually be caught by the remaining layers. Attributing the event to a single active failure or a single latent condition ignores the alignment.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A department's quality program reviews both an airway rescue that succeeded and a similar event that produced harm. What should the analysis primarily examine?
options: The harmful event alone, as success teaches little
Outcome severity scores for each case
questions.explanation: Quality improvement examines the processes, structures, and conditions that shaped both outcomes, since a successful rescue can reveal the same hazards as a harmful one. Focusing on discipline drives reporting underground, studying only harm wastes near-miss learning, and ranking severity does not explain why the events happened.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: An anesthesia service tracks PONV, reintubation, and other outcomes for external quality reporting. Why can these measures influence operations beyond internal improvement?
options: They can tie to standards and payment
questions.explanation: Quality measures support internal improvement and benchmarking, and they can also feed accreditation standards and payment incentives or penalties, which is why they affect operations. They supplement rather than replace peer review, and they are not used to set individual salaries or malpractice coverage.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: Which two items are among the NHQDR core quality areas? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: The National Healthcare Quality and Disparities Report tracks patient safety, person-centered care, care coordination, effective treatment, healthy living, and care affordability. Workforce diversity, accreditation, clinician wellness, and IT adoption can influence quality, but they are inputs rather than core NHQDR quality areas.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A health system expands vaccination clinics and smoking-cessation programs. Which NHQDR core area is being addressed?
questions.explanation: Healthy living emphasizes prevention, health promotion, and behaviors or services that reduce future disease burden. Vaccination and smoking cessation therefore fit this domain rather than treatment of an already established acute illness.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A hospital initiative targets medication errors, falls, and healthcare-associated infections. Which NHQDR core area most directly encompasses these goals?
questions.explanation: Medication errors, falls, and healthcare-associated infections are preventable harms that occur during the delivery of care, so reducing them falls under the NHQDR patient safety area. Care coordination concerns transitions and communication between providers, healthy living covers prevention such as vaccination and smoking cessation, and affordability concerns cost.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A hospital's postoperative sepsis rate is 12.5 per 1,000 operations. If it improves by the same 31.9% reported nationally, approximately what rate would remain?
questions.explanation: A 31.9% reduction leaves 68.1% of the original rate. Multiplying 12.5 per 1,000 by 0.681 gives about 8.51 per 1,000, which rounds to approximately 8.5 per 1,000.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: Opioid prescribing restrictions were implemented, yet overdose deaths continued to rise. Which trend best explains why prescription limits alone had only modest impact?
questions.explanation: Restricting prescription opioids addresses only one source of exposure, and illicitly manufactured fentanyl and other synthetic opioids became the dominant driver of overdose deaths. Prescription-focused measures alone could not address that shift.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A pediatric anesthesia practice is addressing rising anxiety and depression among adolescents. Which group is described as having the most limited access to mental-health treatment?
questions.explanation: National data show especially limited mental health treatment access among low-income and Hispanic youth, reflecting barriers such as cost, insurance, language, and stigma. Privately insured and non-Hispanic White adolescents have comparatively better access, and urban residence alone is not the described gap.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A patient with kidney failure asks which treatment offers the preferred long-term replacement option but remains available to relatively few eligible patients because of access limitations. Which treatment is described?
questions.explanation: Kidney transplantation generally offers superior long-term survival and quality of life compared with remaining on dialysis for eligible patients, but organ scarcity, eligibility barriers, referral, evaluation, and other access constraints limit how many patients receive a transplant.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: Which insurance group was reported to experience a higher burden of healthcare costs in the cited findings?
questions.explanation: The cited findings reported a higher healthcare cost burden among people with private insurance, driven by premiums, deductibles, and copayments. This reflects that specific dataset rather than a universal rule, since an individual's burden depends on plan design, income, and use of care. Uninsured patients face access barriers that the cited cost measure handled differently.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: Cited 2021 data show US life expectancy of 76.1 years versus 82.4 years in comparable peer nations. What is the approximate gap?
questions.explanation: Subtracting 76.1 from 82.4 gives a gap of about 6.3 years, a large difference for nations with similar incomes. Life expectancy changes over time and by source method, so the figures should stay anchored to 2021. Excess deaths from overdose, injury, heart disease, and other causes drive much of the gap.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: Which four causes contribute importantly to premature US mortality compared with peer nations? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Comparative mortality data show that unintentional injury including overdose, heart disease, liver disease, and suicide drive much of the excess premature death in the United States relative to peer nations. Alzheimer disease and influenza cause many deaths, but they occur mostly at older ages and do not explain the premature-mortality gap.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: When prioritizing population-level perioperative risk reduction, which condition remains the leading cause of death in the United States in the cited material?
questions.explanation: In the cited U.S. mortality material, heart disease is the leading cause of death. The question is intentionally anchored to that dataset because rankings and counts can change across years.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: An opioid stewardship program cites national mortality data to justify overdose prevention. Which ranking for unintentional injury, driven largely by overdose, supports this?
options: Third, after heart disease and cancer
Fifth, after stroke and lung disease
questions.explanation: In recent national data, unintentional injury, driven largely by drug overdose, ranked third among causes of death after heart disease and cancer, which supports overdose prevention as a perioperative priority. Rankings shift by year and classification, so the figure should be tied to the dataset period.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: Two patients receive equivalent medical care, but one has unstable housing and no transportation and experiences worse outcomes. What principle does this illustrate?
options: Outcome gaps reflect care quality differences
Outcome gaps mainly reflect patient adherence
Social factors can outweigh clinical care
questions.explanation: Health outcomes depend on social and structural conditions as well as medical care, and some estimates attribute most outcome variation to factors outside the clinic. Here care was equivalent, so care quality cannot explain the gap. Unstable housing and no transportation affect recovery, follow-up, and medication access, not just attendance, and blaming adherence ignores those barriers.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: Which four items are Healthy People 2030 social-determinants-of-health domains? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Healthy People 2030 groups social determinants into economic stability, education access and quality, health care access and quality, neighborhood and built environment, and social and community context. Genetics and personal behaviors shape health too, but they are not social-determinant domains in that framework.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A patient misses preop testing because transportation is unaffordable. Which social-determinant domain is most directly involved?
questions.explanation: Being unable to afford transportation is a financial resource barrier, placing it primarily in the economic stability domain. It also impairs healthcare access, showing how social determinant domains interact.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A patient lives in an area without a pharmacy and with unsafe walking routes. Which social-determinant domain best fits?
questions.explanation: Pharmacy availability, transportation infrastructure, walkability, and neighborhood safety are features of the physical environment in which a patient lives. They therefore fit the neighborhood and built-environment domain.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A patient cannot understand discharge instructions because of low health literacy. Which social-determinant domain is most directly involved?
questions.explanation: Health literacy is closely linked to the ability to obtain, understand, and use health information and is addressed within education access and quality in this framework. Clinically, instructions should still be adapted to the individual's communication needs rather than assuming literacy from education level.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A patient scheduled for outpatient surgery lives alone, lacks transportation, and cannot afford medications. When should these barriers be identified?
options: On the morning of surgery in preop holding
questions.explanation: Living alone, lacking transportation, and being unable to afford medications can make an ambulatory plan unsafe, so they are identified during preoperative care coordination when disposition, escort, and prescriptions can still be arranged. Discovering them the morning of surgery or at discharge often leads to cancellation or an unsafe discharge.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: An anesthesia department standardizes evidence-based protocols across both its main hospital and rural satellite. Which equity priority does this most directly support?
questions.explanation: Standardizing evidence-based protocols at the main hospital and a rural satellite reduces unwarranted variation, which serves the ASA equity priority of quality care for all populations. Access to pain management, maternal care, and insurance access are separate ASA equity priorities that this protocol change does not directly target.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: An AHRQ report lists 250 quality measures. If Black patients received worse care than White patients on about 40% of them, how many measures is that?
questions.explanation: Forty percent of 250 is 0.4 × 250 = 100 measures. The 40% figure comes from the cited AHRQ disparity data for Black, American Indian, and Alaska Native patients and summarizes population-level differences, so it should not be applied to every measure or every encounter. Choosing 40 confuses the percentage with the count.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: Which two postoperative safety measures were cited as showing worse care for Black adults? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: The cited disparity data show worse rates of postoperative sepsis and postoperative pulmonary embolism for Black adults, among other measures. PONV, hypothermia, urinary retention, and dental injury are perioperative outcomes but were not the cited disparity measures, and disparities reflect structural and clinical factors rather than a biologic racial cause.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: An audit finds Black and Hispanic women with similar labor pain scores receive epidural analgesia less often than White women. What disparity does this demonstrate?
options: More epidural requests by minority women
Less epidural access for minority women
Lower pain severity in minority women
questions.explanation: Lower epidural use among Black and Hispanic women with similar pain scores is a disparity in access to neuraxial labor analgesia. It should prompt examination of access, counseling, institutional, and clinician factors rather than assumptions about preference.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: Why can lower epidural use during labor matter when an emergency cesarean becomes necessary?
options: GA may be needed, with airway risk
The epidural must first be removed
Cesarean must wait for epidural placement
questions.explanation: A working labor epidural can usually be extended quickly for cesarean delivery, but without one, an urgent cesarean may need general anesthesia, with added airway, aspiration, and awareness risk in pregnancy. Spinal anesthesia remains possible when time allows, and an emergency cesarean is not delayed to place an epidural.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A maternal care committee notes pregnancy-related mortality two to three times higher among Black women than White women. Which explanation do the cited data support?
options: Higher cesarean rates by patient choice
Differences in tolerance of labor pain
questions.explanation: National data report pregnancy-related mortality about two to three times higher among Black and American Indian or Alaska Native women, and the disparity reflects clinical conditions, access to care, and social and structural factors. Race is not a biologic cause, and patient choice of cesarean or pain tolerance does not explain the gap.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A program ensures patients with sickle cell disease receive timely and adequate analgesia in the ED and OR. Which ASA equity priority does this most directly address?
options: High-quality perioperative care for all populations
questions.explanation: Ensuring timely adequate analgesia for patients with sickle cell disease directly addresses equitable access to pain management. The clinical goal is treatment based on pain and medical need rather than stereotypes or nonclinical patient characteristics.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: Black patients with long-bone fractures receive less analgesia than White patients with comparable injuries. Which factor is cited as contributing to this disparity?
options: True biologic differences in pain perception
Higher addiction rates among Black patients
Lower pain scores reported by Black patients
False beliefs about biologic pain differences
questions.explanation: Research has documented false beliefs among some clinicians about biologic racial differences in pain and tolerance, which contribute to undertreatment. Race is not a biologic determinant of pain, addiction risk does not justify the gap, and the disparity persists when reported pain scores and injuries are comparable.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: Poorly controlled acute postoperative pain can contribute to which THREE clinically important harms? (Select 3)
options: Predictable progression to opioid use disorder
Greater risk of persistent postsurgical pain in susceptible patients
Pulmonary complications from splinting and ineffective cough
questions.explanation: Poorly controlled acute pain causes splinting and weak cough, limits mobility and rehabilitation, and raises the risk of persistent postsurgical pain in susceptible patients. Pain drives sympathetic tone and stress hormones, so tachycardia and hyperglycemia are expected, and untreated pain does not predictably cause addiction.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A patient with sickle-cell disease has frequent crises and repeatedly receives fragmented episodic pain treatment across different facilities. Which resource highlighted by the ASA best supports coordinated longitudinal management?
questions.explanation: Specialized sickle cell centers coordinate hematology, pain, preventive, and acute care across encounters rather than treating each crisis in isolation. Longitudinal coordination matters when fragmented care leads to inconsistent analgesia.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A pediatric ED finds that Black children with appendicitis and pain scores of 8 receive analgesia less often than White children with the same scores. What is the best department response?
options: Attribute the gap to differences in pain tolerance
Reduce analgesia for each child equally
Rely on each clinician's case-by-case judgment
questions.explanation: A 2015 study found Black children with appendicitis and moderate-to-severe pain were less likely to receive analgesia, a disparity driven by bias rather than biology. Standardized orders tied to pain scores reduce the room for biased judgment. Reducing analgesia for each child equally lowers care quality, and pain tolerance does not explain the gap.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A rural hospital lacks pediatric anesthesia specialists and is caring for a young child with an active URI. Why can this create an equity concern?
options: Rural centers do more pediatric cases
URI risk is unrelated to provider skill
questions.explanation: Young children, especially with an active URI, have higher perioperative respiratory risk, so pediatric anesthesia expertise matters. When that expertise is concentrated in larger centers, rural children may receive less specialized care, which is an equity concern. Experience lowers the rate and severity of respiratory events, so provider skill does matter.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: If more than half of uninsured patients are from minority groups, approximately how many of 1,000 uninsured patients would that represent?
questions.explanation: More than half means a proportion above 50%. Fifty percent of 1,000 is 0.5 × 1,000 = 500, so any proportion above one-half represents more than 500 uninsured patients. About 250 corresponds to one-quarter, and about 100 or 50 to one-tenth or one-twentieth.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: An equity review finds that patients with similar PONV risk received fewer antiemetics when they were low-income or uninsured. Which cited study reported this pattern?
questions.explanation: A 2018 registry analysis by Andreae and colleagues found that low-income and uninsured patients with similar PONV risk were less likely to receive antiemetic prophylaxis. Goyal (2015) reported racial differences in analgesia for children with appendicitis, Hoffman (2016) documented false beliefs about biologic pain differences, and Todd (2000) described ED analgesia gaps for Black patients.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: Which four barriers can limit access to quality care beyond insurance status? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Insurance is one access factor, but lack of paid sick leave, low health literacy, language barriers, and distrust of the health system can each block care even when coverage exists. Being uninsured and high-deductible coverage are real barriers, but they are insurance factors and the stem asks for barriers beyond insurance status.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: Which two APSF strategies operate primarily at the individual clinician level? (Select 2)
options: Tie department bonuses to equity metrics
Provide financial incentives for equity measures
Create a systemwide culture of equity
questions.explanation: Recognizing one's own bias and pursuing education are actions an individual clinician can undertake directly. They differ from organizational levers such as governance, institutional culture, measurement, and financial incentives.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: Which three APSF strategies are primarily system-level interventions? (Select 3)
options: Use financial incentives tied to equity measures
questions.explanation: Culture, organization-wide training, and incentive structures operate beyond a single clinician and can shape behavior across the system. System-level equity work also commonly includes measurement, accountability, governance, and process redesign.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A CRNA notices she gives shorter explanations to patients with limited English proficiency. Which AANA-recommended action is the most direct first step?
questions.explanation: The first step is recognizing that communication differs by a nonclinical characteristic, which is implicit bias, and then correcting it with a qualified interpreter and full explanations. A single course does not change the behavior by itself, family interpreters compromise accuracy and confidentiality, and shortening explanations for everyone worsens care.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A CRNA completes one cultural-sensitivity course and says the work is finished. How does the AANA frame cultural humility instead?
questions.explanation: Cultural humility is a lifelong process of self-reflection, awareness of one's own limits, and learning from patients and communities. It cannot be completed with one course, a hiring check, or a certificate, because new patients, beliefs, and biases keep arising throughout practice.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: Which two AANA recommendations most directly strengthen the nurse-anesthesia workforce and practice environment? (Select 2)
options: Partner with community groups on outreach
Collect outcomes data by demographic group
Encourage diverse students to consider nurse anesthesiology
questions.explanation: Recruiting diverse students into nurse anesthesiology and building cultural-competency training into practice act directly on the workforce and the practice environment. Outcomes data collection, community outreach, Medicaid advocacy, and transportation support are equity efforts aimed at measurement, communities, or policy rather than the workforce itself.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A CRNA arranges a qualified interpreter before anesthesia consent. Which AANA recommendation is being applied?
questions.explanation: Arranging a qualified interpreter addresses linguistic barriers and supports accurate two-way communication during consent. It respects autonomy and avoids relying on family members or assumptions about English proficiency.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: Which four principles make up the classic biomedical-ethics framework? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: The classic four-principle biomedical ethics framework consists of autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, and justice. The principles often overlap, so a clinical decision can satisfy or create tension among more than one at the same time.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A regional block is selected because it is expected to improve recovery and reduce opioid exposure, with risks judged acceptable. Which ethical principle is most directly expressed by acting to promote the patient's welfare?
questions.explanation: Beneficence is the positive obligation to promote the patient's welfare. Choosing a regional technique because its expected benefits improve recovery and reduce systemic opioid burden is an affirmative action for patient benefit, provided its risks are acceptable.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A CRNA avoids a medication that previously caused a serious reaction and selects a safer alternative. Which ethical principle is most directly reflected?
questions.explanation: Non-maleficence is the obligation to avoid or minimize preventable harm. Avoiding a drug with a prior serious reaction and choosing a safer effective alternative directly reflects that duty.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A competent Jehovah's Witness refuses blood products after informed discussion. Respecting the refusal most directly upholds which principle?
questions.explanation: Autonomy protects a decisionally capable patient's right to make informed choices about their own body, including refusal of recommended treatment. A competent refusal of blood products should therefore be respected after the implications and alternatives are discussed.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: An uninsured patient receives the same analgesic options and attention as a VIP patient. Which ethical principle is most clearly upheld?
questions.explanation: Justice concerns fair and equitable distribution of care and burdens. Offering clinically equivalent analgesic options regardless of insurance, status, or social privilege applies the same medically relevant standards to both patients.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A sedative would make workflow easier but meaningfully increase aspiration risk, so the CRNA declines to give it. Which principle is most directly upheld?
questions.explanation: Declining a convenience-based sedative because it meaningfully increases aspiration risk prioritizes avoidance of preventable harm over workflow ease. That is the clearest expression of non-maleficence.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A CRNA withholds information about a serious anesthetic risk from a capable patient because they believe it would only cause worry. Which concept does this represent?
questions.explanation: Paternalism means overriding or bypassing a capable patient's choices for their supposed benefit, for example withholding information to avoid upsetting them. It conflicts with autonomy, which requires honest disclosure and respect for informed decisions.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A patient prefers spinal anesthesia, but the CRNA chooses general anesthesia simply because it is easier and never discusses alternatives. Which principle is most clearly violated?
questions.explanation: Autonomy requires meaningful participation in decisions among medically reasonable alternatives. Choosing general anesthesia solely for clinician convenience without discussing the patient's stated preference prevents informed self-determination.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A department routinely schedules uninsured patients last, creating longer fasting and delays. Which ethical principle is most directly violated?
questions.explanation: Justice is violated when access or timing differs for a nonclinical reason such as insurance status. Routinely placing uninsured patients last creates a systematic burden unrelated to medical priority.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: Which two broad responsibilities are explicitly addressed in the AANA Code of Ethics? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: The AANA Code of Ethics is organized around responsibilities to patients and responsibilities as a professional, along with areas such as society, business practice, and research. Duties to a supervising physician, the schedule, payers, or practice partners are not organizing categories of the code.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A CRNA stops positioning because a patient's dignity is being compromised by unnecessary exposure. Which Code principle best applies?
questions.explanation: Stopping to prevent unnecessary exposure during positioning protects privacy and dignity while supporting comfort and safety. The patient-first principle requires that convenience or routine not override these basic interests.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A CRNA observes an unsafe medication practice by a colleague and reports it despite interpersonal discomfort because future patients could be harmed. Which professional principle is most directly demonstrated?
questions.explanation: Advocacy includes speaking up when a practice threatens patient rights or safety, even when doing so is uncomfortable. Reporting a recurring unsafe medication practice protects current and future patients rather than treating the issue as merely interpersonal.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A CRNA uses simulation, continuing education, and competency assessment to remain capable of managing rare perioperative crises. Which professional obligation is being fulfilled?
questions.explanation: Rare crises require skills that decay without deliberate practice. Simulation, continuing education, certification, and competency assessment support lifelong maintenance of the knowledge and psychomotor abilities needed for safe anesthesia care.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: An audit shows pain is assessed differently across demographic groups, and a CRNA changes practice to apply the same clinical standards consistently. Which Code principle is most directly reflected?
questions.explanation: Fairness requires more than identical wording in a policy; it requires consistent clinically appropriate standards and attention to biased implementation. Correcting demographic differences in pain assessment therefore reflects active application of fairness.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A competent patient must choose between two reasonable anesthetic approaches with different risks and benefits. Which Code principle most directly requires enough information for the patient to make that choice?
questions.explanation: Informed consent requires disclosure and understanding of relevant risks, benefits, alternatives, and the opportunity to choose voluntarily. When two reasonable anesthetic options exist, adequate information is what allows the patient's autonomous preference to guide the decision.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A senior CRNA mentors students, maintains certification, and models professional conduct. Which Code responsibility does this best reflect?
questions.explanation: Mentoring, maintaining competence and credentials, and modeling ethical conduct extend beyond responsibility for a single patient. They reflect the clinician's broader professional obligation to sustain standards and support the profession.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A patient-experience redesign wants to cover the complete recognized framework of patient-centered care rather than only communication and comfort. How many dimensions are included in that framework?
questions.explanation: The commonly taught Picker-derived patient-centered framework contains eight dimensions. The question tests recognition of the complete framework rather than implying that every institution must organize its patient-experience program using exactly the same labels.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: Which four items are dimensions of patient-centered care? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Patient-centered care includes respect for preferences, coordination, information and education, physical comfort, emotional support, involvement of family and friends, continuity, and access. Standardized pathways and efficient encounters can support quality, but they center the system rather than the patient's needs and values.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A CRNA explains each step of induction to an anxious patient and answers questions. Which patient-centered-care dimension is most directly reflected?
questions.explanation: Explaining each step and answering questions gives the patient understandable information, which fits the information, communication, and education dimension of patient-centered care. It also provides emotional reassurance.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A CRNA gives PACU a detailed handoff including the pain plan and unresolved concerns. Which patient-centered-care dimension is most directly reflected?
questions.explanation: A detailed PACU handoff transfers the treatment plan and unresolved concerns across settings and clinicians, preserving continuity through a care transition. It prevents the receiving team from having to reconstruct the plan.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A CRNA actively warms the patient and pads pressure points. Which patient-centered-care dimension is most directly reflected?
questions.explanation: Maintaining warmth and preventing pressure injury directly address the patient's bodily comfort during care. These actions fit physical comfort even though they also contribute to physiologic safety.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A child's parent is allowed to remain for mask induction when appropriate. Which patient-centered-care dimension is most directly reflected?
questions.explanation: Allowing a parent to stay for a child's mask induction, when appropriate, involves family in the care experience and can reduce the child's anxiety. Safety and workflow still determine when it is suitable.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: Which four issues are specifically addressed in AANA informed-consent guidance? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: AANA informed-consent guidance addresses when consent is obtained, emergencies, situations where information is withheld, and literacy or language barriers, since each affects whether consent is valid. The anesthetic technique is chosen with the patient rather than by the surgeon, and a second CRNA co-signature is not a consent requirement.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: Which three patients require special attention during anesthesia consent because capacity, pain, or communication may complicate the process? (Select 3)
options: A patient with limited English proficiency
A patient having the same procedure as last year
An anxious adult who asks many questions
A laboring patient in severe pain
A patient accompanied by an adult child
questions.explanation: Severe labor pain impairs attention and deliberation, dementia can impair decision-making capacity, and limited English proficiency requires a qualified interpreter. Anxiety and many questions show engagement rather than incapacity, a repeat procedure still needs consent but poses no special barrier, and an adult child cannot consent for a capable patient.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A patient with limited English proficiency needs anesthesia consent. Which approach best supports valid informed consent?
options: Use a family member for rapid translation
Provide a translated form to sign
Speak slowly in English with diagrams
questions.explanation: A qualified medical interpreter supports accurate, confidential, two-way discussion of risks, benefits, alternatives, and questions. Family members may omit or alter information, a translated form without discussion does not confirm understanding, and slow English with diagrams cannot reliably convey risks to a patient with limited proficiency.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A surgery center wants to simplify its consent form by omitting some state-required elements. Which standard governs whether that is acceptable?
options: All applicable legal and facility rules
questions.explanation: Consent requirements come from overlapping federal, state, accreditation, and institutional sources, so a facility must meet each applicable rule and cannot drop a legally required element for convenience. Facility policy can add requirements but cannot override state law, and accreditation standards are only one layer.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A laboring patient is in severe pain when epidural consent is discussed. Which issue makes this a special consent situation?
options: Labor pain removes capacity to consent
Pain and urgency can affect consent
A partner must co-sign during labor
Only written consent is valid in labor
questions.explanation: Severe labor pain and urgency can affect attention and comprehension, so consent is given in short, clear terms, ideally discussed early in labor, with time for questions. Pain does not automatically remove capacity, a partner's signature is not required for a capable patient, and documented verbal consent can be valid.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A patient with dementia is scheduled for hip surgery. What should happen before relying on the patient's signature alone?
options: Defer to the family's wishes regardless
Assess capacity; use a surrogate if needed
questions.explanation: Dementia does not automatically remove decision-making capacity, which is specific to each decision and must be assessed. If the patient can understand, appreciate, reason, and express a choice, the patient consents; if not, the legally authorized surrogate decides using the patient's values. Family wishes do not override a capable patient.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: An unconscious patient needs emergency surgery and no surrogate is available. How is consent generally addressed?
options: Delay until a court order is obtained
Emergency consent under law and policy
Obtain consent from the charge nurse
questions.explanation: When treatment is needed at once to prevent serious harm and neither the patient nor a surrogate can consent, emergency doctrine and institutional policy allow treatment to proceed. Waiting for a court order or a surrogate delays lifesaving care, and a charge nurse has no authority to consent for the patient.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A health system adapts communication, interpreter access, and policies to patients' differing health beliefs while maintaining the same safety standards. Which concept best describes this approach?
questions.explanation: Culturally competent care adapts communication, interpreter access, and policies to differing beliefs and languages while keeping evidence-based safety standards. Identical communication or unadapted care can fail patients with different needs, and assuming beliefs from ethnicity is stereotyping rather than competence.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: Which two harms can result from poor cultural competence? (Select 2)
options: Higher malpractice premiums for the clinician
Patients may avoid or distrust care
questions.explanation: Poor cultural competence leads to miscommunication and to patients avoiding or distrusting care, which can delay treatment and worsen safety. Malpractice premiums and equipment failures are not direct effects, interpreter services tend to be underused rather than overused, and consent requirements do not change.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: Staff are trained to adapt communication to patient beliefs and to use interpreters appropriately. What outcomes is this culturally competent care intended to improve?
questions.explanation: Effective cross-cultural communication and language access improve understanding and trust, reduce communication errors, and help address disparities. It often takes more time and more interpreter use rather than less, and its goal is care adapted to need rather than uniform care.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A patient's culture discourages direct eye contact, and the CRNA adjusts communication without compromising care. What does this demonstrate?
questions.explanation: Adapting communication after learning a patient's eye-contact norms shows respect for diverse beliefs while keeping clinical standards. It is not paternalism, since no choice is overridden, and asking about preferences avoids assuming beliefs from ethnicity. Consent standards stay the same.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: Under the Belmont Report, which THREE ethical principles guide research involving human participants? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: The Belmont Report names respect for persons, beneficence, and justice, which shape consent, risk-benefit review, and fair subject selection. Non-maleficence is folded into beneficence in the report rather than listed separately, and fidelity and veracity are ethical principles in clinical practice but not Belmont principles.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: Which four protections are fundamental to ethical human-subject research? (Select 4)
options: Right to withdraw at any time
questions.explanation: Voluntary participation, privacy, confidentiality, and the right to withdraw at any time protect autonomy and welfare in research. Research does not promise therapeutic benefit, and requiring completion once enrolled would violate the right to withdraw.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A CRNA proposes a prospective study of a new antiemetic regimen. Which body must approve and oversee the human-subject research?
questions.explanation: An institutional review board reviews and oversees human-subject research, including risk, consent, privacy, and participant protection. The pharmacy and therapeutics committee manages the formulary, quality improvement projects follow a different pathway, and the ethics committee consults on clinical dilemmas rather than approving research.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: Which FOUR groups are covered by specific federal subparts or commonly require additional safeguards in human-subject research? (Select 4)
options: Pregnant women, human fetuses, and neonates
questions.explanation: HHS regulations have subparts for pregnant women, fetuses, and neonates, for prisoners, and for children, and adults with impaired decision-making capacity commonly need added safeguards. Older age with intact capacity or a controlled chronic illness does not by itself make a participant vulnerable.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A researcher wants to enroll sedated ICU patients who cannot provide consent. Which ethical issue is most important?
options: Consent can come from the ICU nurse
Deferred consent fits any ICU study
A vulnerable group needing added protection
No IRB review is needed if minimal risk
questions.explanation: Patients who cannot consent have limited ability to protect their interests, so enrollment needs added safeguards such as permission from a legally authorized representative and IRB oversight. A bedside nurse cannot consent for research, deferred consent is allowed only in narrow circumstances, and minimal-risk research still needs IRB review.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A research consent form explains the study drug but omits its possible harms. Which required element is missing?
questions.explanation: Valid research consent must describe reasonably foreseeable risks and potential benefits, along with the purpose, procedures, alternatives, confidentiality, and the right to withdraw. Omitting the harms leaves participants unable to make an informed choice. Funding amounts, credentials, and enrollment targets are not required elements.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A CRNA studies disparities using IRB approval and de-identified data. Which participant protection is most directly supported?
questions.explanation: De-identifying data weakens the link between research information and a participant's identity, which protects confidentiality and privacy. Voluntariness and the right to withdraw concern how participants enter and leave a study, and beneficence concerns the balance of risks and benefits.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: Which two topics are among recent APSF perioperative patient safety priorities? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: APSF priorities include safety in non-operating room locations and perioperative delirium and brain health, along with medication safety, communication, and clinician safety. Drug costs, PACU throughput, case volume, and on-time starts are operational goals rather than patient safety priorities.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A serious allergy is lost during OR-to-PACU handoff and the patient later receives the allergen. Which APSF safety priority most directly targets this failure?
questions.explanation: An allergy identified correctly but lost during transfer of care is a communication and handoff failure. Standardized handoffs and closed-loop confirmation of critical information keep high-risk facts from being lost between teams.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: During a stable anesthetic, ETCO2 rises subtly from 36 to 42 mmHg before any alarm threshold is crossed. The CRNA notices the trend and investigates immediately. Which human-performance capability is most directly demonstrated?
questions.explanation: Vigilance is sustained readiness to detect small, unpredictable changes before they become crises, and noticing a subtle ETCO2 trend before any alarm is a direct example. Waiting for alarm limits or trusting automation would have delayed recognition, and investigating a new trend is the opposite of fixating on one variable.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A CRNA integrates the patient's prior BP, the current trend, and the expected effect of aortic clamping. Which concept best describes this mental model?
questions.explanation: Situational awareness combines perceiving current data, understanding what they mean, and projecting what will happen next, so integrating baseline pressure, the current trend, and the expected effect of aortic clamping is a time-based mental model. Vigilance detects random changes without that projection, and closed-loop communication concerns team messages.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: During a crisis, a CRNA keeps troubleshooting the monitor as the cause of low SpO2 while ignoring clinical signs of a disconnected circuit. Which cognitive error is this?
questions.explanation: Fixation error is persistent focus on one explanation or task despite evidence pointing elsewhere, sometimes summarized as 'this and only this' or 'everything but this.' Stepping back, verbalizing the problem, and inviting team input help break it.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A provider becomes accustomed to automation and waits for alarms rather than actively scanning waveforms and trends. Which human-factors hazard has developed?
questions.explanation: Automation can reduce workload but can also breed complacency, so clinicians wait for alarms instead of scanning waveforms and trends. That passive monitoring reduces vigilance. Alarm fatigue is desensitization to frequent alarms, and fixation is persistent focus on one explanation despite contrary evidence.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: Loud OR music masks the pulse-oximeter tone and delays recognition of desaturation. Which distraction type is primarily responsible?
questions.explanation: The competing sound directly interferes with perception of an auditory monitor cue, making auditory distraction the primary mechanism. The safety consequence is not merely annoyance; masking a changing pulse-oximeter tone can delay recognition of deterioration.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A CRNA looks at a phone during maintenance and misses a monitor change. Which distraction type is most direct?
questions.explanation: Looking at a phone diverts visual attention from the patient and monitors, making visual distraction the most direct category. It can simultaneously add cognitive distraction, but the immediate missed monitor change follows loss of visual attention.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A CRNA prepares medications for the next case while simultaneously monitoring the current patient. Which distraction mechanism is most relevant?
questions.explanation: Preparing medications for the next case requires working memory, planning, and task switching while the current patient still needs attention, which increases cognitive load. That competing workload can impair detection of changes and decision-making.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: Which four strategies reduce distraction during critical perioperative periods? (Select 4)
options: Lower alarm volumes to cut noise
Play music to reduce team stress
Minimize noise during induction and emergence
questions.explanation: Limiting noise and traffic, preserving focus during time-outs, and following alarm-safety protocols protect attention during induction and emergence. Turning alarm volumes down risks missed alarms, and music adds a competing sound during the periods that most need quiet.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: Nonessential conversation begins during a difficult induction while the anesthesia team is managing the airway. Which communication strategy best protects attention during this critical period?
questions.explanation: A sterile-OR interval limits conversation to information needed for immediate patient care during high-risk tasks such as a difficult induction. It reduces competing cognitive and auditory demands while preserving essential closed-loop communication.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: The surgeon starts discussing weekend plans during induction. What should the CRNA do?
options: Politely defer it until after induction
Report the surgeon after the case
questions.explanation: Induction is a high-workload period when airway, hemodynamic, and drug effects change quickly, so unrelated conversation is politely deferred until the patient is stable. Quiet or brief answers still divide attention, and escalating to a report is not the first step when a simple request will protect the critical period.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: Which three department-level policies can reduce distractions? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Device policies, standardized checklists and guidelines, and audits of time-out adherence are department-level controls that shape the environment for every clinician. Mindfulness, caffeine habits, and self-rating are individual strategies that depend on each clinician rather than on policy.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: After a prolonged shift, a CRNA has overwhelming tiredness accompanied by impaired calculation and decision-making. Which AANA concept best describes this state?
questions.explanation: Fatigue becomes clinically important when it degrades cognitive or physical performance, as impaired calculations and decisions after a prolonged shift show. Burnout is a chronic syndrome of exhaustion and cynicism, sleepiness alone may not impair function, and microsleeps are brief lapses of awareness rather than this sustained state.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: Which two findings are classic signs of clinically important fatigue? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: Fatigue slows reflexes and degrades judgment, attention, memory, and decision-making, so a clinician who is awake may still perform unreliably. It tends to blunt rather than heighten alarm response, and caution, tremor, and talkativeness are not classic fatigue signs.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A CRNA has been awake for 26 hours. Which three performance effects should be expected? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: After about 24 hours awake, vigilance, reaction time, and cognition decline and error rates rise, with impairment often compared to legal alcohol intoxication. Caffeine masks sleepiness without restoring performance, the deficit is cognitive as well as motor, and routine tasks also suffer.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: Which THREE strategies are recommended to reduce fatigue-related risk? (Select 3)
options: Rely on caffeine as the main countermeasure
questions.explanation: Limiting consecutive hours, building in breaks, and protecting sleep reduce fatigue at its source. Longer shifts do reduce handoffs, but the added fatigue outweighs that benefit; caffeine helps briefly but does not replace sleep; and fatigued clinicians consistently overestimate their own alertness, so self-assessment is unreliable.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: After a 24-hour shift, a CRNA repeatedly rechecks one drug label and misses a falling blood pressure. Which explanation best fits?
questions.explanation: Rechecking a completed task while missing a falling blood pressure reflects impaired attention allocation and vigilance, which fatigue causes through perseveration and omission. The rechecking is not useful caution, no alarm desensitization is described, and confirmation bias would involve favoring evidence for a diagnosis.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: Which three items are links in the chain of infection? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: The chain of infection includes an infectious agent, reservoir, portal of exit, mode of transmission, portal of entry, and susceptible host. Breaking any link can reduce transmission.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A CRNA performs hand hygiene and dons gloves before manipulating an IV. Which chain-of-infection link is being interrupted?
questions.explanation: Hand hygiene and gloves reduce transfer of organisms between contaminated sources, hands, equipment, and patients. They therefore primarily interrupt the mode-of-transmission link, although proper aseptic technique can also protect portals of entry.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A chemotherapy patient with ANC 300 is scheduled for port placement. Which chain-of-infection link does this patient most clearly represent?
questions.explanation: Severe neutropenia markedly reduces host defense against infection. The patient therefore represents the susceptible-host link, emphasizing why exposure prevention and aseptic practice are especially important.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: Before the preoperative physical examination begins, the CRNA cleans their hands immediately before first patient contact. Which WHO hand-hygiene moment applies?
questions.explanation: WHO Moment 1 is hand hygiene before touching the patient. Cleaning hands immediately before the preoperative physical examination protects the patient from organisms carried on the clinician's hands.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A CRNA is about to insert an arterial line. Which WHO hand-hygiene moment applies immediately beforehand?
questions.explanation: WHO Moment 2 occurs immediately before a clean or aseptic procedure, such as arterial line insertion, which breaches the skin and enters the vascular system. Hand hygiene is required even if the clinician touched only this patient.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: After handling blood-contaminated tubing, the CRNA removes gloves. Which WHO hand-hygiene moment now applies?
questions.explanation: WHO Moment 3 follows body-fluid exposure risk. Gloves do not replace hand hygiene, so hands should be cleaned after removing gloves used for blood-contaminated tubing.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: After completing a physical examination and before moving to the clean anesthesia workstation, which WHO hand-hygiene moment applies?
options: Moment 5: after touching patient surroundings only
questions.explanation: WHO Moment 4 is after touching a patient. Cleaning hands before moving from the patient examination to a clean anesthesia workspace helps prevent organisms acquired from the patient from contaminating equipment and medications.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: The CRNA adjusts the patient's bed rail and bedside equipment without touching the patient, then leaves the area. Which WHO hand-hygiene moment applies?
questions.explanation: WHO Moment 5 applies after touching patient surroundings, such as bed rails and bedside equipment, even without direct patient contact. These surfaces carry organisms that can transfer to the clinician's hands.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A CRNA intubates, then immediately reaches into the clean anesthesia cart without changing gloves or cleaning hands. Which contamination principle is violated?
options: Intact gloves keep the cart clean
A dirty zone contaminated a clean zone
Hand hygiene is due at case end
Glove change is due after extubation
questions.explanation: Airway manipulation contaminates gloves with oral secretions, so reaching straight into the clean cart moves organisms from a dirty zone to a clean one. Gloves are removed and hand hygiene done before touching clean supplies. Intact gloves still carry organisms on their surface, and waiting until extubation or case end lets contamination spread.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A CRNA touches a clean drug drawer and then a clean syringe on the same workstation. Both are designated green zones. Is hand hygiene required between these two contacts?
options: No, not for that movement alone
questions.explanation: Moving between surfaces within the same clean zone does not itself create a hand hygiene indication. Hand hygiene is needed when a WHO moment occurs or contamination is suspected.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: Which two actions should prompt hand hygiene before returning to the clean anesthesia workspace? (Select 2)
options: Reading the anesthesia record on screen
Drawing up a drug from a cleaned vial
Picking an item up from the floor
questions.explanation: Cellphones and items from the floor are heavily contaminated, so hand hygiene is needed before returning to clean tasks such as drug preparation. Opening sterile packages, drawing from a disinfected vial, and labeling a fresh syringe are clean-workspace tasks themselves.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A department wants to improve anesthesia hand hygiene. Which approach is most defensible?
options: Clean hands after induction and emergence
Clean hands on a fixed hourly schedule
questions.explanation: Hand hygiene should follow clinical indications such as the WHO moments, aseptic tasks, body fluid exposure, and contact with contaminated surfaces. Fixed times such as induction, emergence, once per case, or hourly miss many indicated moments and add unneeded ones, so they do not reliably interrupt transmission.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: Which four interventions are supported for reducing perioperative infection? (Select 4)
options: Double gloving without changing after airway
questions.explanation: Perioperative infection prevention uses several barriers: patient decolonization when indicated, hand hygiene, disinfecting IV ports before access, and cleaning the anesthesia workspace. Staff antibiotics are not recommended, and the outer glove should be removed after airway management rather than worn on to clean tasks.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A patient develops a superficial incisional infection 20 days after appendectomy. Does the timing fall within the usual 30-day surveillance window for this type of SSI?
questions.explanation: Superficial incisional SSIs are tracked for 30 days after surgery, so an infection on day 20 after appendectomy falls within the window. Longer windows of up to 90 days apply to deep or organ-space infections after certain procedures, often with implants, but an implant is not required for superficial SSI surveillance.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A deep or organ-space infection is suspected 70 days after total knee arthroplasty. How should SSI surveillance timing be determined?
options: All SSI surveillance ends at 30 days
Any implant sets a 90-day window for all
Implant cases are excluded from surveillance
questions.explanation: SSI surveillance windows depend on the operative procedure and infection category, with deep and organ-space infections after certain implant procedures such as knee arthroplasty followed for up to 90 days. The procedure-specific definition is applied rather than one universal rule.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A hospital tracks selected postoperative infections because they can affect quality reporting and payment. Which statement is most accurate?
options: CMS refuses payment for any SSI
Effects depend on the specific program
Only the SSI rate itself is reported
Penalties fall on the surgeon, not the hospital
questions.explanation: CMS does not refuse payment for every SSI, and financial effects depend on the specific hospital-acquired condition, quality reporting, or value-based program involved. Reporting covers more than a single rate, and payment adjustments apply to the hospital rather than to an individual surgeon.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: Incision is scheduled for 0800. Which cefazolin timing best meets prophylaxis guidance?
questions.explanation: For cefazolin and most standard surgical prophylactic antibiotics, administration should generally begin so the dose is completed within 60 minutes before incision. For an 0800 incision, 0700 to 0800 fits that timing window.
questions.sourceTitle: Miscellaneous Topics in Nurse Anesthesia Practice

questions.stem: A patient needs vancomycin for a 0900 incision. Why may the infusion need to begin as early as 0700?
options: Its slow rate takes about an hour
It must finish 2 hours before incision
It must peak before the skin prep
questions.explanation: Vancomycin is infused slowly, over at least about 60 minutes, to avoid infusion reactions, so it is started within 120 minutes before incision rather than within 60 minutes like cefazolin. It does not need to finish 2 hours early, it is not redosed every 2 hours, and the target is an adequate level at incision.
